transcript.text: Okay, folks, it is now 07:00 and time to call to order this regular meeting of the Andover Indian Wetlands and Water Courses Commission on Monday, August 1 at 7PM. I see by the smiling faces on the Zoom call that we have Commissioners Larson and Munro present, as well as myself, Chairman Elliott. Will, don't have anybody else to seat, so we'll move on to changes in order to the agenda. I failed to ask our agent to include a revisit to the Commission's annual report for this meeting, and so I propose to add that to item 8C. Without objection. Second it. Okay, we'll vote on it then. I'll second it. Commissioner Larson. Aye. Commissioner Munro. Aye. And I'll vote aye. So the motion carries 300 to add that to the agenda. Any other changes or proposed changes or additions to the agenda? Okay, if not, then we'll move on to Item four, approval of the minutes from 07/12/2022. Give me a second here while I pull them up to my screen, but I hope everybody's had a chance to renew or to review them. And if you have any corrections or changes to add at this time, please make them known. I have none.
Okay, Mr. Monroe. None. Yeah, then I'll move to approve the minutes of July 12, as presented. I'll second. Okay, moved and seconded. Commissioner Larson. Aye. Commissioner Monroe. Aye.

And I also vote aye. So the motion carries 300. Do we have any public comment? We don't have any applications on the agenda, so I'm not surprised that there would be none. And under new business, as you've noted, we don't have any pending applications to consider tonight, which means we can have a nice short meeting. Okay. Agent Wagner, do you have anything to report enforcement or actions that you've been able to take on your own recognizance?

No, no enforcement, no. No permit approvals for this month. I got, a call from 25 Slider Mill Road that they're starting. That was the one that you guys approved sometime last year, I think. Might have been the year before, actually. It was Yeah. They were waiting for Staddlebrook to dry up again. So they're they're gonna be starting that within the next week or so. So I went over there and took a look. And yeah, it's it's pretty dry. So it seemed like a good time to do that. And then I got two notices from that company. Forgot what their name was, the one that was treating the Andover Lake for weeds. I think you got them too, Chairman Elliott. I'm aware of the fact that they're doing the work. Yeah, they sent the notice they treated it on July 20. And on, well, tomorrow they're treating it. So, that's all I got.
Okay, good. Then we can move on to other business on Item 8A.

Chairman Elliott, I did have one question for Agent Wagner before we went on. Go right ahead. That was in the last minutes that we just approved. On 196 Lake Road, it said you were investigating as to whether or not they needed a nutrient allocation worksheet. How did that come out? Oh yeah, that's

getting worked on actually. Jim's on the case and they're I think they're working on it today actually. Okay. So we'll see see if it changes. I don't think it's gonna change much for the the approval I did, but they're working on it now. So I'll fill you in next month. I'll try and fill you in. Hopefully that'll all be completed. Thank you. Okay,

anything else? Nope. Okay, in that case, we will move on to 8A, vernal pool survey. And I see Hank Gruner is on the call. Hank, do you need the screen or anything like that? Yes, if I could share screen, that would be fantastic. Well, I think Mr. Wagner can do that for you since he's running the meeting. I think I made it so you could share.
I don't know if you could check. Yep. Let me do that. Hold on. Yep. In the process of sharing. Alright.

Let me see if I can get this into actual Woah. PowerPoint. There we go. Alright. There we go. Everybody sees that? Yeah. Yep. Great. I like Good, beautiful. Well, I'd like to thank you, Mr. Chairman, providing the time on the agenda tonight to go through the results of our joint Conservation Commission and Inland Wetlands Commission spring vernal pool survey. And so what I thought I'd do is give you a you know the summary results of what we've you know what we actually found. To ground folks a year ago we worked in partnership with the University of Connecticut to map potential vernal pools town wide using aerial photographs and satellite imagery to you know identify where those potential pools might be. And if I recall, I think we identified 183 potential pools, based on certain signatures on those images. We then reached out to

landowners for permission for those pools that were on private land to survey because the intent was to survey pools townwide as many as we could on both private and public land. That was done and completed, and now we're and then we the final phase was to conduct spring surveys, biological and habitat assessments at the pools where potential pools where we had access, with a goal of confirming if in fact they were vernal pools based on the biology there, and also to determine if they were vernal pools to collect some biological and habitat data that could be used both by the Inland Wetlands Commission in reviewing applications,

but also could be used by the Conservation Commission as it moves forward with a broader natural resource inventory mapping, you know, critical resources in the town in preparation for our 2025 plan of conservation and development. So that's kind of where we are. We had, we ended up with 18 participating landowners and 15 participating volunteers. As you recall, a goal of this was to train volunteers from the town to be able to conduct the biological surveys and to, you know, to help so that we could cover a fair number of areas. Was based on work that was done in seven towns back in the early 2000s in the in the Farmington River Valley, where there was an evaluation of the ability of adult volunteers to collect vertical specific data. So we followed very similar to the methodology and the approach to that to that project. We ended up serving 124 potential vernal pools, and again those at this stage they were still potential pools. Because to confirm a vernal pool, really have to do it based on the biota, and obviously you can't see that from analysis of aerial photographs and satellite images. So we had 124 potential pools that we had access to out of I think a hunt, you know there was a 183 or so that we actually initially mapped. That included 51 mapped pools and 26 new pools that we identified during the survey. So, did identify quite a number of new pools that we did not find when we did the GIS analysis, the satellite imagery. And we also had six additional potential pools that in the process of going through the aerial images, we identified six that we had missed previously

on the aerial images, which we were able to go out and conduct some surveys. So, long and short of it is we confirmed 77 pools based on the biology and 47 that were not vernal pools. The primary reason for a pool not being a pool was mostly, I would say the majority of them, probably greater than 90%, where they were too shallow. They were depressions usually associated with other wetlands or along a water course that did not hold water long enough to support the biological activity necessary for fertile pool obligate species. We did have a couple of false positives with conifer trees that we thought were pools, turned out to be a hemlock tree, and a couple that were shadows. One was a ledge shadow that showed up that looked like a pool on an image, and another was a tree shadow. And then we had a few that were turned out to be ponds. The opposite of not holding water long enough, they hold water permanently, so they don't support the typical biological community associated with fertile pools, which have a temporary hydrology to them. Then of course there were, and this was sort of anticipated, especially we were somewhat conservative when we were identifying potential pools, wanting to, you know, not miss some. We knew that there were areas that would be too shallow, and we knew that there were areas that would probably be ponds, but we wanted to hit them anyway. There were 92 pools that we initially mapped that we did not have access to, so we're not able to survey.

There were a couple that we did have access to, but actually just couldn't get to because of some flood conditions or some extremely thick vegetation or a combination thereof. So by and large, a 124 potential pools were surveyed, 77 were confirmed this fertile pools and 47 not. The surveys really were broken at the primary focus of the spring survey was to look at the biological value of the pool, And this is based on the work by Calhoun and Clemens in 2005, where they put together a method that's fairly widely used in the Northeast and here in Connecticut. It's called the best development practices for conserving vernal pools. It was targeted at collecting some basic habitat data and biological data to inform municipal commissions to more effectively conserve pools. So that's the methodology that we were following. There were some slight deviations that we made additions, and I'll explain those as I go through and why. But pretty much we're following the core principles set forth in their biological surveys and habitat surveys. And the focus of the biological surveys in their in that plan is to look at the for the presence of any state listed species that might occur in the pools, or what are called vertical indicator or obligate species. And those are a series of amphibians and one shrimp freshwater shrimp called the fairy shrimp that require vertical pools, so they're determined to be obligate species.

So we're looking for the presence of them, and then we're trying to get a sense of their abundance, and that's where the egg mass counts come in. In this case, particular other, at least 25 egg masses, although we tended to try to count as many egg masses as we could to get a better idea So, the spring surveys focused on those biological surveys. The first survey, we have to time those surveys based on the breeding activity for the amphibians as they move forward in the spring. Luckily, this spring followed an almost ideal trajectory where the breeding season started on target and did not shut down with inclement weather and continued in a very typical fashion, which actually is not so typical or in in New England. We were lucky in the fact that we could time the survey very effectively and we we hit it just as they were. The species were starting to breed.

So the first survey that we worked with volunteers, their focus was to was a March survey. They had to complete the first survey of the vernal pool in March with a focus on identifying where their wood frog egg masses in the pools. And trying to get a count of those egg masses. Second survey whispered targeted for April because spotted salamanders tend to breed a little bit later and have a more protracted breeding season. So the second survey focused on spotted salamander egg masses. Are they present and trying to get an abundance count of those? In addition, the volunteers did not do this, but I did this. I visited all the pools and I did a dip net survey both during March and April to look for the presence of marbled salamander larvae. And the reason we did not have the volunteers do that is that's more difficult technique to do. It's harder for identification, And also, there's a potential to spreading disease if you're running a lot of dip nets through a multitude of vertical pools. So I was able to do that by using multiple dip nets and doing a disinfecting protocol between surveys so it controlled the number of people who were doing that. So I did that in both March and April surveys. All surveys, both the volunteers and myself, we would look for the presence of state listed species. You know, did we encounter certain turtles or snakes or certain species that we would note their occurrence because that obviously is important to know.

And then I added based on some recent literature and recent studies that have been coming at, I was curious on how widely distributed another species of salamander the four toed salamander was, although it's not. An obligate vertical species, it does breed in certain vertical pools, where there's sphagnum swamp growing and we're look based on the research that we're seeing, that's a species that we may need to focus on in the future because of changing environmental conditions associated with our wetlands. So I thought it was a good opportunity to collect information on the presence of that species that are in some of these systems as well. So here is a here's sort of what we found. This this graph shows you by the different species, the percentage of vertical pools that they occurred in. With the wood frog they were widely distributed they occurred in 96% of the vertical pools that we confirmed Spotted salamanders a little less widely distributed in 66% of the vertical pools. That's not necessarily surprising. Wood frogs have a very short breeding season, so they're able to use pools that dry up earlier, so they can be you tend to find them in a broader

range of vertical pool hydrologists than you do spotted salamanders, which have require the pool to hold water for a longer period of time. Marbled salamanders and fairy shrimp were very limited in distribution. The marbled salamander only in 5% and the fairy shrimp in 4%. I believe, certainly with the marbled salamander, that may be an under representation. The previous year we had a very wet fall and the breeding conditions were odd for marbled salamanders. They generally breed when the pool dries up in the fall in the in the dry pool bottom. If you recall from last summer into the fall, was very wet and our pools were pretty much topped out in the fall and we're not sure how marbled salamanders reacted to that. I did note there were a couple of pools where previously I have identified marbled salamanders breeding where we did not find larva.

So I don't know whether the abundance was just low and we were missing them or whether they skipped the breeding season. That species can do that. I've documented that in Andover at several sites where they'll be absent for up to three years in certain pools. So they may be more widely distributed than what this data shows. Fairy shrimp are a crapshoot. We don't really know a lot about them. There's been not been a lot of work on them. I'm a bit surprised that they weren't found in a bit more, but that's consistent with the work that I've done throughout the state and then in and also here in Andover on their occurrence. State listed species we found were spotted turtle, wood turtle, and ribbon snake, and that we found those in about 10% of the pools that we serve. As far as relative abundance, you'll see that it varies by the species again. The red bars are the spotted salamanders and the blue bars are the wood frogs. And this is the number below the less than 25, 25 to 49, 50 to 99, and greater than 100 are the number of egg masses. So for example, 57% of the pools that we surveyed with spotted salamanders, the egg masses were less than 25 total egg masses versus 38% of the the pools that wood frogs occurred in. They tended to have larger egg mass counts.

So you see that that was very variable and varied widely. As far as the range, it's extremely variable. For the wood frog, found as few as two egg masses in a pool and as many as seven zero one, with an average of 110, although a median is probably a better representation because the data is pretty, pretty widely skewed, so median's probably a better representation of that number. Spotted salamanders as few as one egg mass in a pool to as many as 530. This, again, is not surprising. The numbers of the twos and the ones are likely colonizing attempts.

These are species that will attempt to colonize new sites, so you will have adults that will try to breed and reproduce in small numbers in pools, they're rarely successful, although sometimes these pools can establish as populations.
So this isn't necessarily surprising the range in numbers that we that we encountered here. Hank, did it surprise you that on those wood frogs, had a lot over 100 and a lot 125,

but not so much in the middle? No, not really. You'll see some of the reasons, I think, why that shakes out a bit as we go through it. This is the and I apologize. I know these are smaller maps. The if you look on the left, this is the distribution and abundance of wood frogs, and the map on the right with the the green dots is the spotted salamander distribution and abundance. And the dots are scaled based on those those egg mass parameters. So in other words, the larger dots those bigger blue dots or green dots you see are the ones that are generally over 100. And if you do notice if you're familiar with the town, you see Route 6 cutting through the upper corner there and you can see Andover Lake and Bishop Swamp. If you're familiar with the town, notice that those large dots tend to be concentrated up in the Nathan Hale State Forest area and down around the Bishop Swamp area and the large tract of land that includes town land and the Ladano parcel north of Boston Hill Road, where there's lots of forest land still heading into Bolton, and then some areas along the Hop River. And if you look at the Hop River, especially in that central area of the Hop River, there's some very large tracts of forested land that abut the river. You see a similar pattern with the spotted salamanders and what that this is sort of what we see from a conservation standpoint point.

When you have large intact areas of forest, you will have larger both you know abundance and distribution of those species. So that's not surprising at all that that that's where they tend to occur in those larger intact forest areas. But keep in mind, as you'll see, Andover is still a very rural town. We still have a lot of fairly large intact forest systems, so you'll see that play out in a little bit as well. The marbled salamander and the fairy shrimp, as I said, are a little more confounding. The marbled salamander, I don't know why. They all seem to be concentrated North Of Route 6.

That's where the populations were again in the along the Hop River Corridor and then in the Bishop Swamp or the Nathan Hale site. Why we don't have records down in the Bishop Swamp area? I don't know, but I've been surveying Andover for close to forty years now. You know, out of work that I do statewide, but since I live in Andover, I put a lot of time in here, and that that coincides with my, you know, with data that I have for for the town. Why they're not as widely distributed or whether we're just missing them, I don't know, but you know, that seems to be playing out. I do think they're probably more widespread than than those dots indicate

because they, you know, they can skip years and they're a little harder to effectively survey for because they're harder to detect and require a little bit more of a survey effort. As I mentioned with the fairy shrimp, a little surprised that the northern one along Nathan Hale, all of the records I previously had were associated with the Hop River system. But again, we don't know a lot about fairy shrimp and their distribution, and they're a hard one to really again hard to detect, And we don't really know a lot, it's hard to make make a heck of a lot of sense out of out of the data that we have here. State listed species distribution We identified three state species. The yellow dots are the spotted turtle, which was the more widely distributed.

The green dots are the wood turtle, much confined to the Hop River system, and that would be true. Hop River and its tributaries. That's primarily where they occur in the town, and the blue open circle one is the ribbon snake. Both the spotted turtle and ribbon snake occur much more widely in town than this data indicates. I know that from wetland surveys in general. They use a variety of wetland habitats. They're not obligate the vernal pools. And also remember these are state listed species, so detection of them is, you know, very dependent on luck when you're going out just one or two times, Unless you're specifically surveying for these species with multiple effort, they're harder to detect. So these were incidental occurrences that were picked up by myself and volunteers, but they give us some additional information about those vernal pools. But from a conservation planning standpoint, with both the spotted turtle and the ribbon snake, a broader range of our vernal pools will support them for sure, and their species that use a larger landscape. So they're using vernal pools selectively during the season, as well as other habitats. The wood turtle is is widely distributed within the Hop River System and several of its larger tributaries

but doesn't occur as much as you get up into the upland area so its primary area, not surprisingly, is associated with the Hop River System. I mentioned the four toed salamander before, and I was very curious about this one. We we detected it in about 25% of the pools there. This one I didn't ask the volunteers to do because detecting it is you really have to look through. You cover search under logs around the pools, or you look for the females that deposit their eggs in sphagnum tussocks. These are moss that grows on these tussocks of sedge, and you part the sphagnum and you can find them with their eggs. Actually, George, your chairman, was was on one of the surveys where we found found a female

in the in a vernal pool over with the by the Bishop Swamp Wildlife Management Area, where with a female with some eggs. Really cool. Yeah, it's pretty neat. They originally back in the 70s when folks started to first look at this, were considered a rare and endangered species in Connecticut. But what we found out when we first started surveying for them fairly heavily heavily, they're actually more widely distributed statewide, and I find them fairly widely distributed in swamps in Connecticut and vernal pools in in in Andover as well. But the reason I I I wanted to put attention on this one is there's been some recent modeling based on climate change scenarios and their predictions are a little startling. They're looking at a potential 79% decline in this species based on changes to the wetland systems that they use under those climate change scenarios, and Connecticut falls within that decline area. So, I thought it wise to start to get a little bit more baseline data on them while we had the opportunity because it may be a species if those scenarios start to play out that we really need to pay a bit of attention to. I don't find any evidence of decline in them in any of the work that I've been doing statewide over the past years. And we just mapped this species for a for a publication we did with the state, and it was still very, very widespread with the exception of high elevations, but always wise to get the data. So we did collect information on the species. So that's the biological surveys, but there were a second set of surveys that were required to put additional information into the data into the mix to be able to work on the conservation of the pools,

but I did not ask the volunteers to do this because this is a bit trickier. This is looking at the critical terrestrial habitat that surrounds the vertical pools because the vertical pools don't function on their own. They're the breeding habitat for species that are using surrounding terrestrial, primarily forested habitat around them. So I followed again the same protocols in Calhoun and Clemens 2005, where we look at the critical terrestrial habitat zones. But in addition, I took the opportunity as I was visiting all the pools to collect information on the depth and estimated hydro period, and the hydro period is the estimate of how long the pool will potentially hold water. Does it dry up in early spring, say by June, or mid summer or late summer? That's important because it determines its effectiveness to support various biota. The size of the pool, the pool type, is it a man made pool like an old farm pond or a burrow pit? Is it a pool that's associated, you know, that's a classic rural pool isolated depression? Is it a floodplain pool? So different types of pools. The connections to water courses and wetlands, is it associated

with any other wetland system or water course on the landscape? What's the vegetative structure? Is it a diverse vegetation? For example, does it have sphagnum moss which would support certain species like four toed salamanders? Or is it less diverse? What is the bottom substrate? So I collected some of this information to be able to help categorize the pools in addition to looking at the terrestrial habitat zones. So this is what the terrestrial habitat zones look like. This is a pool I as an example, this is Wheeling Road up off of the this is part of the Nathan Hale State Forest. And if you look at the yellow dot that's identifying the exact location of a pool that we confirmed the little dark area around the yellow dot is the pool. And I can actually very accurately measure using GIS what I which I did on the pool sizes. But if you look at the light red ring around the the whole pool, that's that 100 foot immediate conservation zone, and that's a zone that we know that's very critical. It needs to be forested and impacts in that zone can have a significant impact on the water quality, but also on the on the biota associated with that pool because they use that immediate 100 feet. And then the larger buff colored ring that goes out around that is the second zone that extends from 100 to seven fifty feet beyond the 100 foot zone beyond the red zone. And that zone we know is the zone, the primary area where 95 of the the salad, you know, the salamanders and frogs and the organisms that are using that pool for breeding are tending to utilize that habitat. So in this example, you see that there's really no impacts on the immediate pool or the 100 foot zone at all. It's completely protected,

but in the 77, 150 foot zone there's moderate impacts. Mean, I would say minimal impacts you see Wheeling Rd cuts into it, and then you see 123 housing residents that you know that have carved out some area in the forest, but that's really a small minimal impact on that whole habitat corridor. What I also would point your attention to is note that this seven fifty foot zone intersects with several other hundred seven fifty foot zones of vertical pools just to the South of it, some of which are on Bishop Swampland or not Bishop Swamp Nathan Hale State Forest land and further south. We also have some that are on private land, so you see that there's overlapping

connectivity between these habitats and these populations will mix, And that's very important in planning, as you'll see later on. So this is how we mapped those terrestrial zones so that we can look at the condition of these habitats based on current development. And also now we layer in the biological data and we can get a sense of you know what's in that pool and how abundant it is, what's in the pools near it, so on and so forth. So when we do that, what we do with through the protocol of Callum and Clemens, ask a series of questions. There was biological data and that habitat data and depending on how many we answer. We come up with a tier ranking We have a pool either as Tier one through three Tier one pools are high value. In other words, they tend to have a very intact. Habitat, in other words, very minimal development within their either either zone, terrestrial zone.

They have presence sometimes of of of state listed species. They certainly have presence of obligate vertical species using more than one species and or an abundance of those species. Tier two are kind of intermediate. They could have a small number of abundance or a single species breeding in them, or they could have some impacts to the terrestrial habitat zones or both. They're kind of intermediate and then Tier three pools are ones that either have some significant development. There's impacts associated with them, or there could really be no impacts or development. It could be that they're very ephemeral and have very low abundance of species or a single species in it. So the ranking goes from a Tier one through a Tier three. So when we apply that to the pools that we the 77 pools that we collected data on, you see that we come up with 74% of our pools are Tier one pools. Only 3% are Tier two. And 19% are Tier three pools. Three are unknown simply because we were not able to collect enough data because of the the characteristics of the pool to evaluate it. Couldn't get accurate egg mass counts, so we really don't know and we could have missed the species as well.

It's not surprising in a in in a still rural town that we have a lot of Tier one pools. Now I also caution this is probably skewed data somewhat because remember, we were surveying both public and private pools, but our access to private parcels was much more limited than to public. So pools that may already have had impacts on private lands, we didn't necessarily have access to. So this data is somewhat skewed because it includes a, you know, a high number of public pools and some that are going to tend to be more intact systems, and those intact systems also tend to have higher abundance and so forth. So a little bit of caution in interpreting the data. This is how it shakes out when you map it. The yellow dots are basically the Tier one pools, the Tier three pools are the purple dots, the green dots are the Tier two pools, and the red dots are the unknowns. So again, you see concentrations in the you know the forested areas of Tier one pools. It's not surprising you get a fair number of the purple Tier threes along the Hop River, because if you think about that from a physical standpoint, that's a floodplain zone. So you get many areas that are small depressions that'll hold water for a short period of time. So they function, they can, you know, have a couple of egg masses,

but they dry up quick. So it's not unusual in floodplain habitats along those major rivers to get a fair number of tier three pools because of the floodplain characteristics that you don't have in the upland pools, say of of, you know, the the the northern part of town or the southern part of the town. The ones more associated in the interior are more associated with impacts to those pools or isolations to those pools, those are tier threes. But remember, we can't lose sight of the fact that we can't just focus on the 77 pools that we're able to confirm, because there's still a body of pools that we were not able to gain access to. So when we map those, those are all the blue dots now. They there, while we don't have data on them, we do know that there's a potential occurrence of pools there, so we need to keep that as a data set for future use in our planning because they could they, you know, they may well support populations, and they may be important to from a connectivity standpoint to the pools that we have already identified. So there is still a very important data layer not to lose sight of. And when we put it all together, we map in the obligate state vernal pool species, the state listed species, the potential pools of seven fifty habitat zones, which kind of show up kind of funky there, know that's the light buffer around the whole thing. You can start to see some of the values of these larger intact systems And remember, this is just the vernal pool data sets

from the Conservation Commission standpoint. We're layering in this information with a much broader natural resource inventory that looks at other wetland habitats, other terrestrial habitats, like early succession habitat, which is important for biodiversity, other species data, soils data, a variety of other information, farmland data, important farmland soils. We're layering all of that in to be able to help identify core areas in the town where we need to be mindful as we continue to plan, both from a management standpoint, whether it's forestry applications or agriculture or recreational or potential future development, where we can plan accordingly to try to balance those needs with conservation of our biodiversity, including the vernal pool species. I'll also note here while I don't have the the outlines of our three. Open space corridors that have been identified in in in town. They are the wet the Western Corridor which falls pretty much down from the Bishop Swamp area and goes up through the north. This aligns very strongly with that corridor. The Hop River corridor, which obviously follows the Hop River and the Eastern Corridor, which basically all that area that you see with the big dots is all part of that Nathan Hale Forest, all part of our Eastern Quarter. So these data sets align very strongly to those open space corridors,

which were identified by the way in the previous plan of conservation development 2015. A couple of other things just to mention that come out of this that are important for consideration. Notice I circled that 64% of the pools that we identified were connected to other wetland or water courses. One of the things that became very evident as we were going through the pools is very often they were situated in a forested area along a seepage corridor that spanned throughout a forested area. Oftentimes you would literally could follow that seepage corridor and you would hit the depressions, so they're very much connected to other wetland systems in the in the in that we have within our in our forest as well as those water core systems. That's important when we think about it for planning because you know that that from a corridor standpoint that becomes very, very important to consider for ecological connectivity, but also for potential impacts up and downstream within those corridor systems. The other thing I want to note is while many of our pools were forested pools, there were some that were man made because believe it or not, made pool, you know, old farm ponds and places like that. In fact, there was one area in over by the Bishop Swamp area on the backside where it was some old forest roads where the the road was cut in so deep where there was a where there were very abundant egg masses in the in the in the tire ruts. Were holding water for an enormously long period of time and actually functioning as had higher numbers of egg masses than the natural pool that was within 100 feet of it.

So it goes to show you that you know these animals can adapt to some of those type of systems. Some man made pools can function very highly. What I want you to notice is the ones that I circled the 56% the open emergent and open shrub pools.
